paragraphs: This paper studies how two opposing agents can learn strategies in a zero-sum Markov game, where one agent’s gain is the other’s loss. It develops natural actor-critic algorithms and analyzes how many samples they need to approach a Nash equilibrium. The analysis covers the tabular setting, where states and actions are represented explicitly.

The algorithms use two stages and require the agents to agree on an interaction protocol before learning begins. That coordination is feasible in settings such as self-play. During interaction, however, agents observe the joint reward and next state without accessing the other agent’s actions or policy. The analysis combines policy optimization, temporal difference learning, approximate dynamic programming, and stochastic optimization.

The resulting sample bounds improve the best previously known bounds for policy gradient and actor-critic methods in this multi-agent setting, while matching known global-convergence results for single-agent policy gradient methods. Experiments in a two-player bandit environment and Alesia also show improved performance over an optimistic gradient descent-ascent approach. These findings connect theoretical learning efficiency with empirical improvements in the evaluated games.
icml-2022-a-natural-actor-critic-framewo.tldr: Natural actor-critic algorithms improve sample-complexity guarantees for tabular zero-sum Markov games under an agreed interaction protocol.

paragraphs: A model can perform well overall while serving some groups poorly. This paper addresses that imbalance through min-max fairness: training with attention to the group that currently has the worst performance. The objective makes the weakest group’s outcome central to optimization, so improvements in aggregate performance do not define success on their own.

The proposed methods use active sampling and reweighting. Their central rule is straightforward: at each training step, update the model using a data point from the group currently doing worst. Because that group can change as training proceeds, the method repeatedly redirects attention according to the model’s present performance. The formulation applies to classification and regression models trained by minimizing a loss.

The paper also establishes convergence rates for convex learning problems, including linear and logistic regression. These results explain how quickly the proposed procedures approach a min-max fair solution in that setting. The broader practical appeal is the combination of a simple training intervention and compatibility with many loss-based models; the stated convergence guarantees specifically concern convex problems.
icml-2022-active-sampling-for-min-max-fa.tldr: Sampling from the currently worst-performing group provides a simple approach to min-max fairness, with convergence guarantees for convex learning problems.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a neural network must already have some relationship to its target before training can learn efficiently. It introduces Initial Alignment, or INAL, as a way to measure that relationship at initialization. This makes the starting network’s compatibility with the target an explicit object of study, alongside the learning algorithm itself.

The central result is a conditional impossibility statement. For a Boolean target function, a network without noticeable INAL cannot learn in polynomial time using noisy gradient descent with normalized, independently and identically distributed initialization. The conclusion therefore concerns a specified training procedure and initialization setting. It identifies insufficient initial alignment as an obstacle to efficient learning within those conditions.

The authors establish lower bounds for descent algorithms on symmetric neural networks using information about the target captured by INAL. Their result implies that architecture design needs to encode some target-relevant knowledge, as measured by this quantity, for efficient learning in the analyzed setting. It also resolves an open problem identified in prior work. The contribution is a necessary-condition result under stated conditions, rather than a claim that alignment alone guarantees successful learning.
icml-2022-an-initial-alignment-between-n.tldr: Under specified initialization and training conditions, insufficient initial alignment with a Boolean target prevents noisy gradient descent from learning in polynomial time.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn from noisy comparisons between pairs of choices. A fully sequential algorithm can revise its next comparison after every result, but that interaction pattern can be inconvenient for applications such as ranking and recommendation. This paper studies how to organize comparisons into a limited number of parallel batches while retaining strong learning performance.

The analysis considers two settings. One assumes a Condorcet winner, an option that wins against each alternative in pairwise preference. The other assumes strong stochastic transitivity and a stochastic triangle inequality, which constrain the relationships between comparison probabilities. For both settings, the authors develop algorithms with a gradual trade-off between the number of batches and regret, the cost associated with inferior choices.

Using only a logarithmic number of batches, the algorithms match the best known sequential regret bounds up to poly-logarithmic factors. A nearly matching lower bound helps characterize how much improvement remains possible within the analyzed problem. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical results. The main implication is that adapting after every comparison is not required to approach sequential performance under these assumptions.
icml-2022-batched-dueling-bandits-4fb94b.tldr: Batched comparison algorithms approach sequential dueling-bandit regret bounds with only logarithmically many batches under two standard preference settings.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium networks offer a way to exchange additional computation for reduced memory use. A defining feature is the repeated application of the same weights. This reuse makes their behavior different from that of traditional networks and motivates a closer look at how the initial weights influence whether training remains stable.

The paper shows that initialization matters beyond the overall scale of the weights. Deep equilibrium networks are sensitive to higher-order statistical properties of the families of matrices used to initialize them. Consequently, choosing an initialization involves more than selecting a magnitude: the structure of the matrices also affects training behavior. The authors identify orthogonal and symmetric matrices as choices that allow greater stability.

This finding yields a practical prescription for selecting initializations that support training across a broader range of initial weight scales. Its significance is that matrix structure provides another way to improve the usable training regime of these models. The stated result concerns increased stability and a wider range of workable scales; it does not assert that either matrix family guarantees successful training in every case.
icml-2022-deep-equilibrium-networks-are-.tldr: Orthogonal or symmetric initial weight matrices can make deep equilibrium networks more stable across a broader range of initialization scales.

paragraphs: Running neural-network predictions can require more computing power than is available locally, motivating deployment on a third party’s hardware. When that party is not fully trusted, the inputs and outputs can reveal the nature of the task being performed. This paper investigates a computationally practical way to obscure that information during outsourced inference.

The proposed strategy, called Connectionist Symbolic Pseudo Secrets, uses Holographic Reduced Representations to create a pseudo-encryption-style defense for a neural network. Its objective is to make the underlying task harder for the third party to determine. The paper frames this as fast, heuristic protection, motivated by the computational demands of protocols that provide provable security.

The reported experiments show robustness against attacks, including threat models that give the adversary unusually favorable conditions. Those findings provide empirical evidence for the defense in the evaluated settings. The distinction between experimental robustness and a security proof is central to the contribution: the method explores what protection a fast representation-based mechanism can provide when the computational cost of provably secure approaches is a barrier.
icml-2022-deploying-convolutional-networ.tldr: A defense based on Holographic Reduced Representations empirically obscures neural-network inference on untrusted platforms using fast, heuristic protection.

paragraphs: Decision trees can overfit, and regularization often changes their structure through operations such as pruning. Hierarchical Shrinkage instead adjusts the predictions of an already trained tree. It moves each leaf’s prediction toward sample averages at its ancestor nodes, using information from progressively broader groups of training examples.

The amount of shrinkage depends on one regularization parameter and the number of samples at each ancestor. Because the procedure operates after tree construction, it is fast, compatible with any tree-growing algorithm, and can accompany other regularization methods. The authors also show an equivalence to ridge regression on a collection of decision stumps associated with the tree’s internal nodes, giving the adjustment a familiar statistical interpretation.

Across extensive experiments on real-world datasets, the method substantially improves decision-tree prediction, including when other regularizers are already used. Applied to individual trees in random forests, it often improves accuracy and interpretability by simplifying and stabilizing decision boundaries and SHAP values. The results show that changing a tree’s predictions can improve its behavior while preserving its existing branching structure.
icml-2022-hierarchical-shrinkage-improvi.tldr: Hierarchical Shrinkage improves trained trees by pulling leaf predictions toward ancestor averages, often benefiting accuracy and interpretability without changing tree structure.

paragraphs: Evaluating synthetic data requires distinguishing several kinds of success and failure. Samples may resemble real data, cover its variety, or simply reproduce training examples. This paper introduces three evaluation components—alpha-Precision, beta-Recall, and Authenticity—to characterize fidelity, diversity, and generalization separately in a framework intended to work across domains and generative models.

The framework connects statistical divergence measures with precision-recall analysis. Its components have probabilistic interpretations and are estimated through binary classification at the sample level. This supports diagnosis of both individual examples and entire generated distributions. Treating generalization as its own dimension makes copying training data visible independently of the balance between realism and variety, which is particularly relevant when the training data are sensitive.

The sample-level construction also enables model auditing. An auditor can assess individual outputs from a black-box generator and discard low-quality examples after generation, improving overall output quality without changing the model itself. The contribution therefore combines a more differentiated evaluation framework with a practical filtering use case. Measuring copying provides a relevant indicator for privacy-sensitive applications, rather than itself establishing a privacy guarantee.
icml-2022-how-faithful-is-your-synthetic.tldr: Three sample-level metrics separate synthetic-data fidelity, diversity, and copying, while enabling post-generation auditing and filtering.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates clustering from the perspective of each individual data point. Its proposed individual preference stability criterion requires a point to be closer, on average, to its own cluster than to any other cluster. This gives a concrete meaning to a point preferring its assigned group, with motivations from game theory and algorithmic fairness.

The authors first show that deciding whether an IP-stable clustering exists is NP-hard in general. They then identify settings where efficient exact algorithms are possible. One polynomial-time algorithm finds an exactly stable clustering for points on the real line. Another efficiently finds a stable division into two clusters when distances come from a tree metric.

The paper also studies relaxed stability, allowing a point’s average distance to its own cluster to be somewhat worse than its distance to another. It supplies polynomial-time algorithms with different guarantees for these relaxations and evaluates selected methods alongside standard clustering approaches on real datasets. The contribution connects an individually meaningful clustering requirement to its computational costs, showing where exact satisfaction or controlled relaxation can be achieved efficiently.
icml-2022-individual-preference-stabilit.tldr: Individual preference stability requires every point to favor its own cluster on average, with efficient algorithms available in restricted settings and for relaxations.

paragraphs: Electronic health records contain patient measurements that vary over time, combine multiple data types, and are often sparse. Grouping similar patient trajectories can help predict disease progression, but useful groups also need clinical meaning. This paper addresses the difficulty of obtaining interpretable clusters when disease outcomes are unevenly represented.

The authors propose a supervised deep-learning model that forms clusters around clinically understandable phenotypes while considering both patient trajectories and outcome prediction. New loss functions address class imbalance and cluster collapse, a failure of the grouping process to maintain meaningful distinctions. A feature-time attention mechanism identifies which variables and time periods are important to the phenotypes associated with each cluster.

The model was tested on two datasets representing different medical settings. The authors report more interpretable cluster formation and improvements of at least 4% over benchmarks on relevant metrics. The result connects predictive grouping with explanations of what distinguishes the groups across time and measurements. Its reported benefits concern the evaluated datasets and metrics, supporting the approach as a way to make trajectory clusters more informative as well as predictive.
icml-2022-learning-of-cluster-based-feat.tldr: A supervised EHR clustering model addresses imbalance and cluster collapse while using feature-time attention to explain patient phenotypes.

paragraphs: Debugging a classifier often means examining incorrect predictions and guessing what went wrong. Conceptual counterfactual explanations, or CCE, aim to make that process systematic by explaining mistakes through concepts people can understand. An explanation might connect a zebra’s faint stripes to its incorrect classification as a dog, making the suspected issue concrete.

The method combines counterfactual explanations with concept activation vectors. This connects questions about changes that would alter a prediction to representations of human-understandable concepts. The authors validate CCE on established pretrained models and report meaningful explanations of their errors. For newly trained models with spurious correlations in the training data, CCE identifies those correlations as the cause of mistakes from a single misclassified test example.

The paper also applies CCE to two challenging medical tasks. Clinicians confirm that the resulting explanations provide useful insights into model biases and mistakes in real-world settings. These findings support conceptual explanations as a tool for investigating errors, rather than leaving developers to infer patterns manually across many failures. Publicly available code is intended to make the approach applicable to additional models.
icml-2022-meaningfully-debugging-model-m.tldr: Conceptual counterfactual explanations connect classifier mistakes to understandable concepts and identify spurious correlations in the evaluated models.

paragraphs: A classifier deployed over time may face changing relationships between inputs and labels. Conventional adaptation often summarizes this change through a single control, such as a learning rate, forgetting factor, or window size. This paper argues that such a scalar treatment misses an important feature of concept drift: different statistical characteristics can evolve differently.

The authors introduce adaptive minimax risk classifiers, or AMRCs, to track these changes in multiple dimensions. Their method uses multivariate and high-order tracking of the evolving data distribution. This allows the adaptation mechanism to account for distinct patterns of change across statistical characteristics, instead of representing all temporal change with one rate.

Alongside adaptation, AMRCs provide computable, tight performance guarantees. The paper evaluates both prediction quality and the reliability of these guarantees on multiple benchmark datasets, reporting classification improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The combined contribution is a richer model of changing data and an accompanying assessment of expected performance. The experimental findings support both parts: improved classification in the evaluated settings and guarantees that reliably describe performance there.
icml-2022-minimax-classification-under-c.tldr: Adaptive minimax risk classifiers track multidimensional concept drift and provide computable performance guarantees, with benchmark improvements.

paragraphs: Some causal effects can be determined from observational data, while others require interventions that actively change the system. Those interventions can be costly. This paper studies how to choose a collection of interventions that makes a desired causal effect identifiable while minimizing the total cost of obtaining the necessary information.

The authors prove that the intervention-design problem is NP-complete. They then connect it to the minimum hitting set problem, using that relationship to develop an algorithm that can obtain an optimal solution or a logarithmic-factor approximation. This connection supplies an algorithmic route for a problem whose general computational difficulty rules out expecting an easy exact solution in every case.

To further address computational cost, the paper proposes several polynomial-time heuristics. These methods can return suboptimal intervention collections, but simulations on random graphs show small regrets. The findings provide both a formal characterization of the design problem and practical methods for tackling it. The heuristic evidence is empirical and concerns the simulated graphs, while the exact and approximation approaches offer different forms of solution guarantees.
icml-2022-minimum-cost-intervention-desi.tldr: Minimum-cost causal intervention design is NP-complete, but a hitting-set connection enables exact, approximate, and practical heuristic approaches.

paragraphs: Retrieval-based language models combine a standard language model with examples fetched from an external datastore during prediction. Searching that datastore can be expensive, especially when retrieval happens at every step. RetoMaton addresses this bottleneck by giving the datastore structure that can be traversed, reducing dependence on repeated nearest-neighbor searches.

The method stores pointers between consecutive datastore entries and groups entries into states. Together, these turn the datastore into a weighted finite automaton, which is traversed alongside the language model during inference. Construction is unsupervised and can use any text collection, including the original training corpus or material from another domain. The automaton approximates the datastore search by exploiting this organization.

The reported results offer two benefits: perplexity can decrease by up to 1.85, or nearest-neighbor searches can be reduced by up to 83% relative to kNN-LM without worsening perplexity. These are alternative reported outcomes, rather than a claim that both maxima occur together. The work shows how a symbolic structure over retrieved examples can improve the quality or computational efficiency of retrieval-assisted language modeling.
icml-2022-neuro-symbolic-language-modeli.tldr: RetoMaton organizes a language-model datastore into an automaton, improving perplexity or reducing nearest-neighbor searches by up to 83%.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether learning dynamics approach stable solutions through their actual sequence of strategies. It extends last-iterate convergence analysis beyond the two-player zero-sum setting and beyond requirements that players follow tightly prescribed, matching learning rules. The results cover several broader game families and different forms of learning dynamics.

For a class including constant-sum polymatrix and strategically zero-sum games, the authors establish bounded trajectories for methods such as optimistic mirror descent, even with different player algorithms and prediction mechanisms. This supports O(1/sqrt(T)) rates and optimal O(1) regret bounds. They also show a qualified alternative: optimistic mirror descent either gets arbitrarily close to a Nash equilibrium or achieves efficiency exceeding the robust price-of-anarchy benchmark.

For potential games, mirror descent reaches an epsilon-equilibrium within O(1/epsilon²) iterations under a broad class of regularizers, and optimistic variants obtain optimal constant regret bounds. The framework extends to near-potential games and unifies analyses of distributed learning in Fisher markets. Additional analysis addresses optimistic gradient descent in general-sum continuous games. These results broaden the settings in which convergence, regret, and efficiency can be understood together.
icml-2022-on-last-iterate-convergence-be.tldr: New analyses extend convergence, regret, and efficiency guarantees to broader game families and heterogeneous learning dynamics.

paragraphs: When participants pool data for Bayesian learning, assigning credit requires measuring what each participant contributes. This paper studies Shapley values in parametric Bayesian learning games. A coalition’s value is measured by the divergence between its posterior and prior distributions, so credit reflects the information gained through combined data.

The main theorem concerns differences in credit between pairs of players. Under regularity conditions, these differences converge in probability to the corresponding Shapley-value differences in a limiting game. That game uses a value function proportional to the log-determinant of joint Fisher information. The result replaces a difficult information-gain calculation with an asymptotic description built from Fisher information.

The authors use this relationship to construct an online collaborative learning framework that is asymptotically Shapley-fair. It avoids expensive posterior-prior divergence computations and instead needs a consistent estimator of Fisher information. Experiments with real-world data demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. The convergence statement is specifically about pairwise Shapley-value differences under the stated conditions, and the fairness property is asymptotic, preserving the distinction between limiting behavior and exact fairness at every stage.
icml-2022-on-the-convergence-of-the-shap.tldr: Under regularity conditions, Shapley-value differences in Bayesian learning approach a Fisher-information-based limit, enabling asymptotically fair collaboration.

paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions as information arrives. Machine-learned predictions can help guide those decisions, but an algorithm may have several predictions available rather than one clear forecast to trust. This paper studies how to use that collection, with performance assessed against the best solution obtainable from the supplied predictions.

The authors provide a generic framework for online covering problems. Its guarantee is competitive relative to the performance of the best prediction-derived solution, making that solution the benchmark for evaluating the online algorithm. The analysis incorporates predictions into a classical potential-based approach, giving a way to reason about their influence throughout the decision process.

The framework is applied to online set cover, weighted caching, and online facility location. These applications demonstrate that the same underlying treatment of multiple predictions can support several established online problems. The contribution is an algorithmic and analytical framework for exploiting available forecasts while comparing performance with the strongest solution they provide. Its stated benchmark is prediction-based; the abstract does not claim that the method always matches an optimal solution with full knowledge of future inputs.
icml-2022-online-algorithms-with-multipl.tldr: A generic online covering framework uses multiple learned predictions and competes with the best solution those predictions provide.

paragraphs: An agent may need to solve many tasks that differ in their reward functions. Successor features allow it to reuse previously learned policies when rewards are expressed linearly, but ordinary reuse does not guarantee an optimal solution. This paper develops a way to learn a policy collection that supports stronger transfer guarantees.

Under mild assumptions, the authors connect successor-feature transfer to multi-objective reinforcement learning. They then extend Optimistic Linear Support to learn policies whose successor features form a convex coverage set. This set provides the coverage needed for generalized policy improvement to construct optimal behavior for new tasks with linearly expressible rewards.

Once that policy collection has been learned, the stated transfer guarantee requires no additional environment interactions or training samples for the new task. The guarantee applies to the specified family of linearly expressible tasks and the framework’s assumptions. Experiments in discrete and continuous domains with value-function approximation show improvements over state-of-the-art competing methods. The key advance is to organize what gets learned in advance so that later policy reuse can support optimality, rather than merely reasonable performance.
icml-2022-optimistic-linear-support-and-.tldr: Learning a convex coverage set of successor features enables optimal transfer to new linearly expressible tasks under the framework’s assumptions.

paragraphs: Differentially private training introduces noise to protect sensitive data, creating a trade-off between privacy and model utility. This paper studies how auxiliary public data from the same distribution can improve that trade-off. Its method uses public data throughout a mirror-descent training procedure, with the public-data loss defining the mirror map and private gradients supplying the linear term.

For linear regression with non-isotropic sub-Gaussian features, the authors prove population-risk guarantees that are asymptotically better than the best known private-training guarantees without public data, provided enough public samples are available. They also establish noise-stability properties that control variance caused by the noise introduced for differential privacy.

Experiments on StackOverflow, WikiText-2, CIFAR-10, and EMNIST demonstrate improved privacy-utility trade-offs. The method significantly improves over traditional DP-SGD without public data and also improves over DP-SGD applied to models pretrained on public data. These results support using public information to shape private optimization beyond initialization alone. The theoretical advantage retains its stated distributional and public-sample-size conditions, while the broader empirical evidence comes from the four evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2022-public-data-assisted-mirror-de.tldr: Public-data-assisted mirror descent improves private training’s privacy-utility trade-off, with conditional regression guarantees and gains on four benchmarks.

paragraphs: Random utility models describe the probability that someone selects an item from competing alternatives. This paper focuses on choices between two items at a time. The input is a tournament matrix whose entries give pairwise selection probabilities, and the task is to find a random utility model that reproduces those probabilities as closely as possible.

The authors develop a polynomial-time algorithm that approximately minimizes average error across pairs. This gives an efficient method for fitting a random utility explanation to observed or specified head-to-head preferences. The objective measures agreement over the collection of comparisons, making the average discrepancy between the matrix and the fitted model explicit.

In experiments, random utility models exactly represent many tournament matrices previously considered in the literature. Across the tested matrices, the largest average error is approximately 0.001. The models are also competitive with earlier approaches on prediction tasks. These findings indicate strong representational ability for the evaluated examples, alongside useful predictive performance. The near-zero error is a result for those matrices, rather than a claim that every possible tournament matrix has an exact random utility representation.
icml-2022-rums-from-head-to-head-contest.tldr: A polynomial-time algorithm fits random utility models to pairwise choice probabilities, achieving very small average errors on the tested matrices.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a surrogate model to guide the search for good values of an expensive function. Gradient observations can enrich a Gaussian-process surrogate, but they also make its kernel matrices much larger. With n observations in d dimensions, naive multiplication costs O(n²d²), while naive inversion costs O(n³d³), creating a substantial high-dimensional bottleneck.

This paper identifies matrix structure arising from a wide range of kernels. Exploiting it permits exact matrix-vector multiplication in O(n²d) for gradient observations and O(n²d²) for Hessian observations. The improvement concerns the cost of these matrix operations, preserving exactness while avoiding the corresponding naive computation.

The authors also develop a structure-aware automatic differentiation method that carries these benefits through transformations and combinations of kernels. It applies to virtually all canonical kernels and extends automatically to more complex examples, including neural-network and spectral-mixture kernels. This matters because computational scalability need not require restricting modeling to one specially derived kernel. The approach supports flexible, problem-dependent surrogate design while making gradient-informed Bayesian optimization more practical at high dimension.
icml-2022-scalable-first-order-bayesian-.tldr: Structure-aware automatic differentiation enables exact, cheaper kernel matrix operations for gradient-informed Bayesian optimization across many kernel families.

paragraphs: Model-agnostic meta-learning, or MAML, trains models for adaptation from a small number of examples. Its optimization has two linked levels: learning within tasks and learning across tasks. This structure can produce a more complicated loss landscape than ordinary empirical risk minimization, potentially including more saddle points and local minima that make optimization challenging.

Sharp-MAML brings sharpness-aware minimization into this two-level setting. The approach makes the sharpness of the loss landscape part of the optimization strategy, addressing the difficulties associated with MAML’s structure. The paper also introduces a computation-efficient variant, so its investigation includes both the proposed method and a version designed to reduce computational demands.

Experiments show that Sharp-MAML and its efficient variant can outperform standard MAML, with a reported example of +3% accuracy on Mini-Imagenet. The authors complement these findings with a convergence-rate analysis and a generalization bound. Together, the contributions provide empirical and theoretical support for applying sharpness-aware optimization to bilevel learning, without implying that every task or training configuration receives the same improvement.
icml-2022-sharp-maml-sharpness-aware-mod.tldr: Sharp-MAML applies sharpness-aware optimization to MAML, showing empirical gains alongside convergence and generalization analyses.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference in models with many parameters faces a trade-off between flexible uncertainty modeling and computational efficiency. Stochastic gradient MCMC can be asymptotically exact, but its sampling chain may explore high-dimensional distributions slowly. Variational inference offers another route, often at the cost of strong assumptions about the posterior’s form and factorization.

This paper combines ideas from stochastic gradient MCMC and coordinate-ascent variational inference in a non-parametric variational scheme. Its Langevin-type algorithm uses a self-averaged posterior energy: some latent variables are averaged using samples collected in earlier chain iterations. This breaks dependencies between coordinates in a controlled way, allowing the chain to mix faster. A dropout-style modification provides additional scalability.

The method is evaluated with ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and FMNIST. In every evaluated case, the authors report improvements in convergence speed, final accuracy, or both compared with stochastic gradient MCMC and parametric variational inference. The contribution offers a way to relax restrictive posterior assumptions while improving practical inference behavior. The stated results do not require both speed and accuracy to improve simultaneously in every case.
icml-2022-structured-stochastic-gradient.tldr: A non-parametric inference scheme uses earlier samples to control coordinate dependencies, improving convergence speed and/or accuracy in the evaluated models.

paragraphs: Standard analyses of gradient descent commonly require a sufficiently small step size. For an L-smooth objective, a familiar condition places that size below 2/L. Yet machine-learning training often uses steps that do not satisfy this condition and still converges, although the path toward convergence can be unstable. This paper investigates that apparent mismatch between standard analysis and observed behavior.

The authors examine unstable convergence from first principles and discuss its key causes. They also identify its main characteristics and study how those characteristics relate to one another. The investigation combines theoretical reasoning with experiments, using both to develop a coherent account of behavior that falls outside the usual small-step analysis.

The contribution is an explanation of a convergence phenomenon, rather than a new optimizer described in the abstract. Its significance is to help reconcile successful training with violations of a condition used by many existing analyses. The observations show that this familiar condition does not cover all convergent behavior encountered in practice; they do not establish that arbitrary larger step sizes will converge for every objective.
icml-2022-understanding-the-unstable-con.tldr: Theory and experiments investigate why gradient descent can converge unstably even when its step size violates a standard small-step condition.

paragraphs: Explaining a Transformer prediction requires identifying how input features contribute to the result. Gradient-based explanations use local information about the model’s behavior, but this paper shows that such information can fail to reliably capture feature contributions. The distinction matters because sensitivity near one input does not necessarily provide a dependable account of the prediction.

The authors identify attention heads and LayerNorm as major sources of unreliable explanations. They propose more stable propagation through these components, producing a method that extends layer-wise relevance propagation to Transformers. The approach directly targets the model operations implicated in the explanation problem, rather than treating the Transformer as an undifferentiated function.

The paper provides theoretical and empirical support that the proposed propagation overcomes the identified deficiency of a simple gradient-based approach. It also reports state-of-the-art explanation performance across a broad range of Transformer models and datasets. These findings support adapting explanation procedures to the internal structure of Transformers. The claimed advance concerns more reliable attribution of predictions in the studied settings, rather than a change to the underlying prediction task itself.
icml-2022-xai-for-transformers-better-ex.tldr: A Transformer-specific extension of relevance propagation improves explanations by stabilizing propagation through attention heads and LayerNorm.
